reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: Occurs when the peripheral iris obstructs the trabecular meshwork, blocking aqueous outflow and raising intraocular pressure, often in hypermetropic eyes with shallow anterior chambers

An acute attack presents as an ophthalmic emergency with a severely painful red eye, blurred vision, haloes around lights, headache, and frequently nausea and vomiting that can be mistaken for an abdominal or neurological problem
Classic signs include a mid-dilated fixed vertically-oval pupil, a hazy oedematous cornea, a shallow anterior chamber, ciliary injection, and a stony-hard eye on palpation
Relative pupillary block is the usual mechanism, in which aqueous is trapped behind the iris, bowing it forward to appose the drainage angle
Gonioscopy of both eyes is essential to confirm a closed or occludable angle and to guide prophylactic treatment of the fellow eye

Initial treatment lowers pressure medically with topical intraocular-pressure-lowering agents and systemic acetazolamide, followed by laser peripheral iridotomy once the cornea clears to re-establish aqueous flow
The fellow eye is at high risk of a subsequent attack and should receive prophylactic laser iridotomy
Chronic angle closure may be insidious and painless, producing progressive optic-nerve cupping and field loss that mimics open-angle glaucoma
reference.pathophysiology: In primary angle closure the peripheral iris comes into contact with the trabecular meshwork and obstructs aqueous drainage, causing intraocular pressure to rise. The commonest mechanism is relative pupillary block, where resistance to aqueous passing between the lens and iris margin lets pressure build in the posterior chamber, bowing the peripheral iris forward against the angle. Predisposing anatomy includes a shallow anterior chamber, short axial length (hypermetropia), a relatively anterior and thick lens, and a crowded angle; pupillary mid-dilation in dim light or with mydriatics can precipitate acute closure. Sustained apposition damages the trabecular meshwork and may form permanent peripheral anterior synechiae, while a sudden pressure spike causes corneal oedema, iris ischaemia, and optic-nerve injury.
additionalDifferentials: Acute conjunctivitis or keratitis causing a red eye
Phacomorphic glaucoma from an intumescent lens
Secondary angle closure from a posterior segment mass or effusion
additionalInvestigations: Gonioscopy of both eyes to assess angle configuration and detect peripheral anterior synechiae
Applanation tonometry to measure the height of the pressure rise
Anterior segment assessment of chamber depth, optionally with anterior segment OCT or ultrasound biomicroscopy
Optic disc evaluation and OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer for glaucomatous cupping
Automated perimetry to document any field loss once the eye settles
redFlags: Acutely painful red eye with haloes, a mid-dilated pupil, and a stony-hard globe indicating an acute attack requiring emergency pressure reduction
Nausea and vomiting misattributed to a systemic cause while the eye is overlooked
Corneal oedema with markedly reduced vision that may become permanent if pressure is not lowered promptly
An untreated occludable fellow eye at imminent risk of its own acute attack
reference.prognosis: Prompt medical pressure reduction followed by laser iridotomy usually aborts an acute attack and prevents recurrence, but delayed treatment can cause permanent optic-nerve damage, peripheral anterior synechiae, cataract, and lasting visual loss. Chronic angle closure carries a substantial risk of progressive glaucomatous field loss if unrecognised.
pitfalls: Attributing the headache, nausea, and vomiting to a gastrointestinal or neurological cause and missing the ocular emergency
Dilating a susceptible shallow-chamber eye and precipitating an acute attack
Failing to examine and treat the occludable fellow eye prophylactically
Assuming laser iridotomy alone controls pressure when extensive synechial closure or coexisting open-angle damage requires further therapy
Overlooking chronic painless angle closure presenting as apparent open-angle glaucoma
